content:
This is very fun! I really like the UI, I think this could be very nice for getting someone to learn the "intuition" behind what Lean is doing (potentially even someone not really used to formal proofs yet).

Some thoughts:

  • After using a "goal-acting" tactic (exfalso) a couple times, it becomes annoying you need to drag it to the goal every time. Making it just work immediately when clicked would be smoother
  • Instead of dragging cases/induction to the context n : Nat, it should work to click on the variable and then be asked which of them you want (less dragging). Similarly, clicking on an equality should offer injection/discrimination if possible. In a way these are the ways of "eliminating" such assumptions, and presenting it like this helps build intuition about what introduction and elimination rules are.
  • I guess in general, having an alternative to dragging would make things much more pleasant, especially on a laptop with a touchpad. I propose having a mode where you click "the thing" and then "where it applies" instead of dragging the thing to where it applies!
  • I wonder how well this scales. It is already a bit unwieldy to select from the multitude of available theorems in the latter part of the game. And sometimes I like doing things like have _ : subgoal := _ which just is not possible with the existing combinators. I guess this also makes it impossible to do induction with more fancy motives? I am not sure if you plan to keep working on the UI but I would be interested in seeing a solution for this :)
  • I encountered a bug:

Bug in level 6 of adv. mult (includes partial solution)


I tried these steps. In step 10, I did induction, because cases did not make progress (it just renamed the variable).

  • I encountered another bug, and used the feedback form for it. It's related to variable shadowing/renaming.
(this is the discussion thread for #Project announcements > Visual Lean @ 💬 )

Not bad, I guess. But then, I feel typing command was never the main difficulty of NNG4, and I feel the overhead of having so many visual elements can fill your brain with irrelevant details.
Visual may beat keyboard at a few tasks, but visual for everything? Too inconvenient.

Reminds me of Scratch.

Would be nice if the data is cached in the browser so you don't need to download 74MB every time.

I wouldn't say this helps people to learn the intuition though. (It elaborate the tactic proofs and typechecks the result.)

Side thoughts: May be nice to have some visual/keyboard hybrid mode: you start with visual, but the program tells you how to achieve the equivalent with keyboard, then after a few times you use keyboard. There is a little issue that you have to either type with one hand, or constantly move your hand between the mouse and the keyboard.

More side thoughts: I feel it would be better if the user is dropped into a real Lean editor with the infoview. There's so much stuff available in the real editor/infoview setting but missing in the game interface.

But someone tries to make a nice game, and I sit here complaining and never finishing my ideas (possibly with AI assistance, but I have AI too)? Not a good position to be in.

user202729 said:

I wouldn't say this helps people to learn the intuition though.

Interesting. I was thinking this could be cool for an "intro to proofs" class where you don't want to overwhelm the students with formalism (or Lean syntactic minutiae) but want to ingrain into them that proofs are "like a game" where at any point in time you can only take so many steps. Why do you think this would fail at this/do you have ideas for how to improve?

Okay, if you say you think it can be cool, I would agree. I was reading it as “understand what Lean does internally” which I don't think so.

For “at each point you can take so many steps”… hm… technically this is not true since you can have anything (the fact that NNG4 didn't introduce have until some time later annoyed me a lot, since have is how one write proof “normally”).

If you want to give students the impression that writing proof is fun, this may work. Or because the visualizable examples are too simple, it may give some students the opposite viewpoint of proof being a pointless game. (I was more interested reading through Mathlib and trying to figure out what is a filter and why it makes sense uniform space is defined in term of that than to work through NNG4 and get confused, but maybe it's just me.)

user202729 said:

you can have anything

yes indeed, this is a somewhat more advanced step which does not really work (yet?) with this UI. (I guess you'd need to add a formula construction mode). But it is still just one of the several steps, and once you take it, you continue in two subgoals.

I played through only a few levels, but I found this very well done. I don't have a comprehensive list of feedback, but I think my biggest discomfort is switching back and forth between the left- and right-hand sides of an equality in the goal. I think it'd be much nicer to have the full equation on one screen, so for instance you can see the nice boxes around expressions for both sides at the same time.
@Johannes Hostert Apologies, I didn't expect anyone to play with trackpad! I'm going to have to think about how to accommodate that
I've gone ahead and fixed some of the bug reports; I'm still in the process of making some of the gameplay quality of life changes

@user202729 My thought process is that as digitised mathematical proofwriting becomes more important over time, we're going to want to teach the principles of intuitionistic logic at the undergraduate or even high school level. There's no reason this should even require a background in writing computer code. I built Visual Lean as an experiment to see how that might work.

I do agree, that for any serious proofs, it's too tedious to work with. But I think some of the 'gestures' I've come up with could be useful for interacting with a Lean proof directly from the infoview, in Visual Studio Code.
@Chris Henson I'm going to look into the full equation editing. On some devices, there's just not enough space (mobile vertical), but I think on desktop there's usually enough space

Okay, but I have one idea how this could be useful not just as a game: integrate it into the infoview. After the user selects a step, modify the source code to add the rw or simp_rw or unfold that works.
(Of course assume the user is experienced and don't need excessive guidance or animation.)

What benefits from such visualization?

  • Lemma searching: if you know what the transformed goal should be and can even type it out, but can't find the lemma to apply, one should be able to just type out the goal and let Lean suggest the rw needed. Even better if one only need to type out the fragment of the goal that needs to change.
  • Interactive unfolding: sure you can unfold ⟨the identifier name⟩, but when it's hidden behind a notation, it isn't clear. (Unfolding can be useful when you see a goal that is not obviously an existential e.g. a ∈ image b, the next step is an use, and it may not be obvious what that step does. Unfolding the ∈ and the image would have clarified that.)

Or (for didactic purpose): have a tactic called help that lists the possible tactics that can be applied at the current state. When one clicks on an option in the infoview, replace the help with the selected tactic.
That way the student will (hopefully?) quickly learn how to be more efficient.
